introduction-the-check-engine-light.core: An alert interrupts a human. It should fire only when something needs action now or soon, and carry enough context to act. Too many alerts cause fatigue and ignored pages; too few cause missed outages. Good alerting is a pipeline: rules evaluate signals, Alertmanager groups, dedups, routes and silences them, and humans get a few actionable notifications with runbooks.

first_principles.problem: On-call engineers receive 300 alerts a week, most self-resolving, and miss the one real outage among them.

analogy.title: A car's check-engine light
analogy.story: It should light up for real problems with a code a mechanic can read, not flicker for every bump in the road.
analogy.breaks: Cars have one light; production has thousands of potential alerts.

check.q: What is the main test of whether an alert should page someone?
check.a: Whether it requires a human to take action now (or soon) to prevent or fix user impact.

symptom-based-vs-cause-based-alerting.core: Cause-based alerts fire on internal conditions (CPU at 90%, a pod restarted, disk at 80%) that may not affect users at all, and they miss failure modes nobody predicted. Symptom-based alerts fire on what users experience: error rate, latency and availability against SLOs. Page on symptoms; route causes to dashboards or low-urgency tickets that help diagnose why a symptom fired.

first_principles.problem: CPU alerts page nightly during batch jobs with no user impact, while an outage caused by a bad config produces no alert.

analogy.title: A doctor treating fever vs every possible germ
analogy.story: Monitoring temperature catches any infection; testing for each germ separately misses new ones.
analogy.breaks: Fever is a single number; services need several SLIs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pages only when users are affected, whatever the cause.

code.text:
- alert: CheckoutHighErrorRate
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
    / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[5m])) > 0.02
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations:
    summary: "Checkout 5xx > 2% for 5m"
    runbook: https://runbooks.acme/checkout-errors

check.q: Why is a high-CPU alert usually a poor page?
check.a: High CPU often has no user impact; it's a cause that may or may not lead to symptoms, causing noisy, non-actionable pages.

alert-rules-in-practice-anatomy-of-a-pro.core: A Prometheus alerting rule has an expr (a PromQL condition that returns series when the alert should fire), for (how long the condition must hold before firing, which filters blips), labels (severity, team, used for routing), and annotations (summary, description with templated values, runbook and dashboard links). Alerts move from inactive to pending to firing, and Alertmanager receives firing alerts.

first_principles.problem: An alert fires on every one-second latency spike because it has no 'for' clause.

analogy.title: A smoke detector with a delay and a label
analogy.story: It sounds only if smoke persists for a few seconds, says which room, and has instructions printed on it.
analogy.breaks: Smoke detectors don't template values; annotations can show the current error rate.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fires only after 10 sustained minutes, with context.

code.text:
groups:
  - name: api
    rules:
      - alert: APIHighLatencyP99
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, service) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.5
        for: 10m
        labels: { severity: page, team: payments }
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} p99 {{ $value | humanizeDuration }}"
          runbook_url: https://runbooks.acme/api-latency
# promtool test rules tests/api_alerts_test.yml

check.q: What does the 'for' clause do in a Prometheus alert?
check.a: Requires the condition to be continuously true for that duration (pending state) before the alert fires.

managing-the-flood-grouping-and-deduplic.core: One incident can trigger hundreds of alerts: every pod, every replica, every dependent service. Alertmanager deduplicates identical alerts from HA Prometheus pairs and groups related alerts by labels (group_by: [alertname, cluster, service]) into one notification. group_wait batches initial alerts, group_interval sets how often updates are sent, and repeat_interval re-notifies unresolved ones.

first_principles.problem: A database failover sends 400 separate pages, one per pod, within two minutes.
truths: Humans need one notification per problem.

analogy.title: A news editor combining wire reports
analogy.story: Fifty reports about the same storm become one headline story with updates.
analogy.breaks: Editors judge relatedness; Alertmanager groups only by labels.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 400 pod alerts → 1 notification listing affected pods.

code.text:
route:
  receiver: default
  group_by: [alertname, cluster, service]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h

check.q: What does group_wait control in Alertmanager?
check.a: How long to wait after the first alert of a new group to collect more before sending the initial notification.

routing-getting-the-alert-to-the-right-p.core: Alertmanager routes are a tree. Each alert walks it matching labels (team, severity, service) to choose a receiver, such as PagerDuty for team-payments pages, Slack for warnings, or email for tickets. Ownership labels must be set consistently in rules or added via relabelling, and continue: true lets one alert notify several receivers. Time-based routes handle business hours.

first_principles.problem: All alerts go to one shared channel, and nobody knows whose problem each one is.

analogy.title: A hospital triage desk
analogy.story: Patients are directed to the right department and urgency level based on their symptoms and tags.
analogy.breaks: Triage nurses improvise; routing trees must cover every label combination.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Payments pages go to payments on-call; warnings to their Slack.

code.text:
route:
  receiver: slack-catchall
  routes:
    - matchers: [team="payments", severity="page"]
      receiver: pagerduty-payments
    - matchers: [team="payments"]
      receiver: slack-payments
    - matchers: [severity="ticket"]
      receiver: jira
receivers:
  - name: pagerduty-payments
    pagerduty_configs: [{ routing_key: <secret> }]

check.q: What happens to an alert that matches no specific route?
check.a: It goes to the root route's default receiver (often a catch-all channel), which should be monitored for unowned alerts.

fatigue-management-silences-and-inhibiti.core: Silences temporarily mute alerts matching labels, during planned maintenance or a known incident, with a creator, comment and expiry. Inhibition rules suppress dependent alerts while a higher-level alert fires: if a cluster is down, don't also page for every service in it. Combined with regular review of noisy alerts (delete, tune or downgrade), they keep pages meaningful and protect on-call health.

first_principles.problem: During a planned database upgrade, on-call is paged 50 times for expected errors.

analogy.title: Do-not-disturb mode and a 'power outage' notice
analogy.story: You mute calls during a planned meeting, and when the building's power is out you don't need separate alarms from every appliance.
analogy.breaks: Do-not-disturb is personal; silences affect the whole team, so they need comments and expiry.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No pages during upgrade; one page if a cluster dies.

code.text:
amtool silence add service=orders-db --duration=2h --comment='CHG-1042 PG upgrade' --author=alice
# alertmanager.yml
# inhibit_rules:
#   - source_matchers: [alertname="ClusterDown"]
#     target_matchers: [severity=~"page|warning"]
#     equal: [cluster]

check.q: What's the difference between a silence and an inhibition rule?
check.a: A silence is a temporary manual mute by labels; inhibition automatically suppresses target alerts while a source alert is firing.
